lines.text: Introduction, section two. A recurring hypothetical.
Imagine you are on the turn in a no-limit hold em pot, and the turn card has just delivered a third club.
You look down at your hand and you have no pair, no flush, and no straight, only the Ace of clubs sitting there as your one and only chance.
That Ace-high flush draw is about a one-in-five shot to hit the nut flush on the river.
Your opponent is stone-faced, giving you no reads, and the clock is ticking on your decision.
The question is simple to ask and famously hard to answer: do you bet, or do you take a free card?
This is the setup we will keep returning to throughout the introduction, because it captures almost every tension we care about.
Betting is appealing because you know your opponent cannot hold the current nuts, and because the Ace of clubs sets up a devastating value bet on any club river.
Checking is appealing because a fourth club can come whether or not you bet, and giving up the option to bluff-catch on the river costs you money too.

The real answer is that at equilibrium you should be indifferent between betting and checking with this exact hand, and that indifference is what forces both players into balanced strategies on later streets.
That single word, indifference, is going to do a lot of work in this book, so keep this hypothetical hand in the back of your mind as we go.
